# The Ramsey Decomposition

The last ingredient of complementation is a combinatorial fact: **every** $\omega$-word factors as
$$ \alpha \in U\,V^{\omega}, $$
a prefix from one class $U$ followed by infinitely many blocks from a **single idempotent** class $V$ (idempotent means $V\cdot V=V$). This holds even when $\alpha$ is **not** ultimately periodic.

The chapter's witness is the non-periodic word
$$ \alpha = \underbrace{abc}_{v_1}\ \underbrace{abcc}_{v_2}\ \underbrace{abccc}_{v_3}\cdots,\qquad v_i = ab\,c^{\,i}. $$
The number of trailing $c$'s grows forever, so $\alpha$ is not ultimately periodic. Yet — because an extra $c$ only loops at $s_2$ — every block $v_i$ has the **same** $\approx_{\mathcal A}$-profile. They all belong to one class $V$, and $V$ is idempotent. So $\alpha=[\varepsilon]\,V^{\omega}$: prefix class $U=[\varepsilon]$, then $V$ forever.

---

```{=html}
<script>
(function(){
  const States=['s0','s1','s2']; const Fset=new Set(['s1']);
  const Delta=[['s0','a','s1'],['s1','b','s2'],['s2','c','s2'],['s2','a','s1']];
  const NONE=0,REACH=1,REACHF=2;
  const empty=()=>{const P={};States.forEach(p=>{P[p]={};States.forEach(q=>P[p][q]=NONE);});return P;};
  function base(sym){const P=empty();Delta.forEach(([p,x,q])=>{if(x===sym){const v=(Fset.has(p)||Fset.has(q))?REACHF:REACH;if(v>P[p][q])P[p][q]=v;}});return P;}
  function ident(){const P=empty();States.forEach(p=>P[p][p]=Fset.has(p)?REACHF:REACH);return P;}
  function compose(R,S){const T=empty();for(const p of States)for(const r of States){if(R[p][r]===NONE)continue;for(const q of States){if(S[r][q]===NONE)continue;const v=(R[p][r]===REACHF||S[r][q]===REACHF)?REACHF:REACH;if(v>T[p][q])T[p][q]=v;}}return T;}
  function profile(w){let P=ident();for(const ch of w)P=compose(P,base(ch));return P;}
  const sub=q=>'s<sub>'+q[1]+'</sub>';
  function gridHTML(P){
    let h='<table class="grid"><tr><th>&nbsp;</th>'+States.map(q=>`<th>${sub(q)}</th>`).join('')+'</tr>';
    for(const p of States){h+=`<tr><th>${sub(p)}</th>`;
      for(const q of States){const v=P[p][q];
        if(v===NONE)h+='<td class="cell-none">&minus;</td>';
        else if(v===REACH)h+=`<td class="cell-reach">${sub(q)}</td>`;
        else h+=`<td class="cell-reachF">${sub(q)}<sup>F</sup></td>`;}
      h+='</tr>';}
    return h+'</table>';
  }
  const eq=(A,B)=>States.every(p=>States.every(q=>A[p][q]===B[p][q]));
  const COLORS=['#30bced','#e08a3c','#8e6fd4','#2ec4b6','#e0578a','#5b8def'];
  function render(){
    const n=+document.getElementById('nb23-range').value;
    document.getElementById('nb23-n').textContent=n;
    // word line
    const wl=document.getElementById('nb23-word'); wl.innerHTML='';
    for(let i=1;i<=n;i++){
      const block='ab'+'c'.repeat(i);
      const wrap=document.createElement('div');
      const b=document.createElement('div'); b.className='blk'; b.style.borderColor=COLORS[(i-1)%COLORS.length];
      for(const ch of block){const c=document.createElement('div');c.className='c';c.textContent=ch;b.appendChild(c);}
      const lab=document.createElement('div'); lab.className='blabel'; lab.textContent='v'+i;
      wrap.appendChild(b); wrap.appendChild(lab); wl.appendChild(wrap);
    }
    const dots=document.createElement('div'); dots.textContent='⋯'; dots.style.fontSize='1.4rem'; wl.appendChild(dots);
    // profiles
    const gs=document.getElementById('nb23-grids'); gs.innerHTML='';
    const profs=[];
    for(let i=1;i<=Math.min(n,3);i++){const P=profile('ab'+'c'.repeat(i));profs.push(P);
      const w=document.createElement('div');w.className='gwrap';w.innerHTML=`<strong style="font-family:ui-monospace,monospace">v${i}=ab c<sup>${i}</sup></strong>`+gridHTML(P);gs.appendChild(w);}
    // check all n equal
    let allEqual=true; const P1=profile('abc');
    for(let i=1;i<=n;i++){ if(!eq(profile('ab'+'c'.repeat(i)),P1)) allEqual=false; }
    // idempotency
    const V=profile('abc'); const VV=compose(V,V);
    const idem=document.getElementById('nb23-idem'); idem.innerHTML=
      `<div class="gwrap"><strong>V (= class of v₁)</strong>${gridHTML(V)}</div>`+
      `<div class="gwrap"><strong>V · V</strong>${gridHTML(VV)}</div>`;
    document.getElementById('nb23-verdict').innerHTML=
      `<div class="verdict-box"><strong>All ${n} blocks share one class V, and V·V = V is ${eq(V,VV)?'confirmed':'FALSE'}.</strong> `+
      `So α = [ε]·V<sup>ω</sup>: prefix class U=[ε], then the idempotent block class V repeated forever — a Ramsey decomposition of a word that is <em>not</em> ultimately periodic. The shared profile sends s₀→s₂ and s₂→s₂ both visiting F (s₁), so the run threads through s₁ in every block: α is accepted.</div>`;
  }
  document.getElementById('nb23-range').addEventListener('input',render);
  render();
})();
</script>
```

Why do the blocks collapse? An extra trailing $c$ only loops at $s_2$ ($s_2\xrightarrow{c}s_2$), which does not change the profile — every $v_i=ab\,c^{i}$ takes $s_0\to s_2$ and $s_2\to s_2$, each visiting $s_1\in F$, and has no path from $s_1$. That is one class $V$, and composing two such blocks yields the same shape, so $V$ is idempotent. This is exactly the abstract decomposition the pigeonhole argument produces in general — here we simply *read it off* the automaton. Saturating on these class products is the final step: **[Notebook 24](24-saturation-complement.qmd)**.
